title: emf and r from two readings or a graph

screens.h: A straight line: y = mx + c
p: emf = V_{load} + Ir can be written **V = (−r)I + emf**.
Plot the terminal pd (y) against the current (x). The **gradient is −r** and the **y-intercept is the emf**.
Each reading of one battery is one point on that line.

rules: Each **state** of the circuit is **one point** (I; V_{load}).
The line through the points is **V = (−r)I + emf**.

screens.q: On a graph of terminal pd (y) against current (x) for one battery, what is the y-intercept?
choices: At I = 0 there are no lost volts, so the terminal pd equals the emf.
r is the size of the gradient, not the intercept.
That is the x-intercept, where R_{ext} = 0.
screens.why: The y-intercept is at I = 0: no lost volts, so it is the emf.

screens.q: The line has a gradient of −2,00 V·A⁻¹. What is r?

traps: r is the gradient’s size, not 1/gradient.

screens.why: gradient = −r, so r = 2,00 Ω. Its unit is V·A⁻¹ = Ω.

p: Take the gradient from **two points on the best-fit line**, far apart and marked on the graph. **Never from table values.**
Extend the line to the y-axis to read the emf.
To read off: at a given current, read V from the line, then R = V/I.

screens.h: Worked example 11.9: the terminal pd against current graph
screens.q: “A student varies the current through the circuit by varying the external resistance, R … and record the reading on the voltmeter across the battery.” Current (A): 0,8; 2,4; 3,2; 4,4; 5,5; 6,3. Voltmeter (V): 18,7; 15,8; 14,1; 12,6; 10,3; 9,0. 8.1.2 Calculate the gradient. (4) 8.1.3 Calculate the internal resistance. (3) 8.1.4 Without a calculation, determine the emf. (2) 8.1.5 What will R be when the current is 4,0 A? (3)

lines.x: Two points on the line: (1,0 A; 18,25 V) and (6,0 A; 9,50 V) ✓

traps: The line slopes down: the gradient is negative.
Δy over Δx, not Δx over Δy.

lines.x: V_{load} = emf − Ir, so V = (−r)I + emf
emf = 20 V ✓. It is the y-intercept: at I = 0 there are no lost volts, so the terminal pd equals the emf ✓.

ask.prompt: Read the emf from the graph.

traps: That is the first reading in the table. Extend the line to I = 0.
That is a point on the line at 1,0 A. Read where the line meets the y-axis.
20 ÷ 4 puts the whole emf across R. Take away r: 5 − 1,75.
20 ÷ 4 puts the whole emf across R. Take away r.

lines.x: Or read off V = 13 V at 4,0 A, so R = V/I = 13/4 = 3,25 Ω.

screens.q: A battery is connected first to a 2,0 Ω resistor (current 2,0 A), then to a 1,0 Ω resistor (current 3,0 A). So emf = 2,0(2,0 + r) and emf = 3,0(1,0 + r). Find r.
screens.why: The same battery has the same emf and r. 4 + 2r = 3 + 3r, so r = 1,00 Ω.

screens.q: Now put r = 1,00 Ω back in. What is the emf?

num.hint: emf = 2,0(2,0 + 1,0). Check with the other equation.

can: Write V = (−r)I + emf and match it to y = mx + c.
Take a gradient from two points on the line, with its unit.
Read the emf at the y-intercept.
Solve two states of one battery for r and the emf.
